# How Avalokiteśvara got its accent back

The ASCII form *avalokiteshvara* is missing something. **Avalokiteśvara** restores the ​marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly ‌record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Devanagari evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By the end, ‌the marks in Avalokiteśvara will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Avalokiteśvara
- **ASCII form:** avalokiteshvara
- ​**Meaning:** "Lord who looks down in compassion"
- **Domain of influence:** Compassion, Mercy, Bodhisattva
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** Preserves stress
- **Original script:** अवलोकितेश्वर (Devanagari)
- **Live domain:** avalokiteśvara.com

## Overview

**Avalokiteśvara** (*avalokiteshvara*) — Compassion, Mercy, Bodhisattva · ​Lord who looks down in compassion — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Compassion, Mercy, Bodhisattva". The name means "Lord who looks down in compassion".

**Avalokiteśvara** belongs ​to the Buddhist tradition, where it is associated with compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Avalokiteśvara** and serves its temple at [avalokiteshvara.com](https://punicodex.com/avalokiteshvara/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature ​— a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists. The plain ASCII form *avalokiteshvara* survives as a modern convenience imposed by ​the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **अवलोकितेश्वर**. Etymologically it means "Lord who ‌looks down in compassion".

Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara, from avalokita 'beheld, looked down upon' + īśvara 'lord'; the bodhisattva of compassion, source-form of Guānyīn and Kannon.

The ASCII form *avalokiteshvara* survives only because the early ​domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Avalokiteśvara** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address ​bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

The letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- **a** → **A** — Same, capitalized
- **v** → **v** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **i** ​→ **i** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **s** → **ś** — Ś: palatal sibilant, atomic letter (IAST ś)
- **h** → **—** — Not written: sh digraph ‌realized as single letter ś
- **v** → **v** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is ​served at **avalokiteshvara.com**.

## Etymology & Roots

The recorded derivation reads: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara, from avalokita 'beheld, looked down upon' + īśvara 'lord'; the bodhisattva of compassion, source-form of Guānyīn and Kannon.

The root gloss ‌is "lord who looks down."

The reconstruction is classed as attested.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **अवलोकितेश्वर**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Avalokiteśvara*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- ​Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara is written in Devanagari as अवलोकितेश्वर
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation ​(ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/avalokiteshvara/** — Buddhist Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **A** — Initial character of the restored form Avalokiteśvara.
- **valokiteśvara** — Remainder of ​the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Buddhist tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'AVALOKITESHVARA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred ​and historical forms of the name:

- **Buddhist** — Avalokiteśvara, the restored Unicode form of the name

Avalokiteśvara preserves both features because the Buddhist form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or ​special characters.

## Mythology

The stories of **Avalokiteśvara** circulate within the Buddhist corpus, where the figure embodies compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Avalokiteśvara is attested in the canonical Buddhist sources as a figure ‌associated with compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Lord who looks down in compassion" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Avalokiteśvara** is the bodhisattva of compassion ​who hears the cries of all sentient beings. In Mahāyāna sutras he descends into every realm to save the suffering, manifesting in forms appropriate to those he teaches. In East Asia he became ‌the goddess Guānyīn, while in Tibet he is the patron bodhisattva manifesting through the Dalai Lamas. The *Heart Sūtra* and *Lotus Sūtra* celebrate his willingness to assume any form—male, female, monarch, or beggar—to ​liberate beings from suffering.

### The Lord Who Looks Down (The Name)

The name is an act of attention: *ava-lokita*, 'perceived, looked down upon,' joined to *īśvara*, 'lord' — the Lord Who Looks Down, ‌as Monier-Williams parses the Sanskrit. The Lotus Sūtra's twenty-fifth chapter, the *Universal Gateway*, turns the etymology into a program: the Buddha declares that whoever calls Avalokiteśvara's name in the moment of terror ​— surrounded by fire, swept by flood, bound in chains, cornered by demons — will be saved, because this bodhisattva scans the world the way a parent scans a crowd for a child. ‌Kumārajīva translated the name into Chinese as Guanshiyin, 'Perceiver of the World's Sounds,' and the translation stuck: East Asia knows him by the listening. The name is the whole doctrine — compassion is ​not a mood but a gaze that never lifts.

### Thirty-Three Forms for Every Kind of Suffering (Lotus Sūtra)

The *Lotus Sūtra* (ch. 25) closes its gateway chapter with a list that reads like ‌a census of the human condition: to beings who can be saved through a Buddha's body, Avalokiteśvara appears as a Buddha; likewise as a pratyekabuddha, a śrāvaka, a king, a householder, a ​government official, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a boy, a girl, a god, a nāga, a yaksha, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kinnara, a mahoraga — the sūtra ​counts thirty-three bodies in all. Śāriputra asks why he is called Perceiver of Sounds, and the answer is simplicity itself: he perceives the world's sounds and responds to each. The list is the ‌myth's meaning: suffering has no shape the bodhisattva will not borrow to reach the sufferer, and mercy wears every uniform the world issues.

### The Eyes and Arms She Gave Away (Princess Miaoshan)

China's ‌most beloved Guanyin legend is also its latest — recorded in the Song-dynasty *Xiangshan baojuan*, the 'Precious Scroll of the Fragrant Mountain.' King Miao Zhuang's youngest daughter Miaoshan refused every suitor and ‌every palace command, asking only to become a nun; exiled and persecuted, she held to her practice while her father's hatred hardened. When the king fell mortally ill, the diviners declared that only ​the eyes and arms of a person without resentment could cure him. A mountain ascetic — Miaoshan in disguise — gave them, and died; as her body was carried off, she was received ​into the Fragrant Mountain, revealed as Guanyin herself, with a thousand hands and an eye in every palm. The late legend gives the bodhisattva's iconography its human face: every hand is a sacrifice ‌once made, and compassion is the scar tissue of self-giving.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Avalokiteśvara concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the ​name:

- **Restored Name** — The Unicode form Avalokiteśvara carries the original marks of the Buddhist tradition.
- **Source Script** — Attested in the original script as अवलोकितेश्वर.
- **Domain** — Compassion, Mercy, Bodhisattva
- **Etymology** — ​Lord who looks down in compassion

- **The lotus** — Purity rising unstained from the mud of samsara — the flower on which he stands above the world he refuses to leave
- **The vase ‌of amrita** — The nectar of compassion in his left hand, poured out drop by drop on the burning places of beings
- **Thousand arms with an eye in each palm** — His vow ​rendered anatomically: a hand for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and saving are one motion
- **Om Mani Padme Hum** — The six-syllable mantra — 'the jewel in ​the lotus' — recited across Tibet, Mongolia, and the Himalaya for a thousand years
- **The blue throat of Nīlakaṇṭha** — The wrathful form's throat stained blue from drinking the world's poison — compassion ‌willing to take on even Śiva's darkest work

## Realm & Domain

**Avalokiteśvara** belongs to the Buddhist tradition, ‌where it is associated with compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

### Compassion

The central domain of Avalokiteśvara in the buddhist tradition.

### Lord who looks down in compassion

The name signifies "Lord who looks down in ​compassion".

### Unicode Restoration

The restoration Avalokiteśvara recovers what plain ASCII avalokiteshvara flattens.

### Original Attestation

Attested in the sources as अवलोकितेश्वर.

### The Universal Gateway

Lotus Sūtra ch. 25: whoever calls his name in fire, ​flood, chains, or the jaws of demons is delivered at once.

### Thousand Arms, Thousand Eyes

His Great Compassion form: an arm for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and ​saving happen together.

### Perceiver of Sounds

ava-lokita, 'perceived, looked down upon': his very name is an act of attention that never lifts.

### Om Mani Padme Hum

His mantra on the lips of half ​the Himalaya — the jewel in the lotus — recited for every suffering being.

## The Unicode Restoration

Avalokiteśvara preserves stress. The ASCII fallback *avalokiteshvara* still resolves everywhere, ‌but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 15 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 2: 2 further adjustments (ś, h). That is the whole thesis ‌of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **avalokiteśvara.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode ‌form as xn--avalokitevara-4rc.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Avalokiteśvara; the machines see the encoding. That duality is ​the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Devanagari can now be typed into any browser on ​earth.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **Avalokiteśvara**, the journey from the ASCII ​fallback *avalokiteshvara* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 15 characters, 13 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. ‌The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **a** stays as it is — Same, capitalized.

The **v** ‌stays as it is — Same.

The **s** becomes ​**ś** — Ś: palatal sibilant, atomic letter (IAST ś).

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set ​of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
